newsitem.title: UK: IRA truce holds new hope for N.Irish peace drive.
newsitem.headline: IRA truce holds new hope for N.Irish peace drive.

text.p: The IRA ordered its guerrillas to observe a truce in their battle against Britain at noon on Sunday, improving prospects for a fresh start in Anglo-Irish efforts to end conflict in British Northern Ireland.

In a decision applauded by the United States, Britain and Ireland, the outlawed Irish Republican Army (IRA) disclosed that it had told all its units to implement an "unequivocal restoration" of an August 1994 ceasefire that lasted 18 months.

"Having assessed the current political situation, the leadership of Oglaigh na hEireann (IRA) are announcing a complete cessation of military operations from 12 o'clock midday on Sunday, the 20th July 1997," its leaders said on Saturday.

It was the announcement that London, Dublin and Washington had been demanding for the past year to salvage peace efforts crippled by guerrilla violence and bitter acrimony between Northern Ireland's rival Protestant and Catholic politicians.
It paved the way for Sinn Fein, the IRA's legal political arm, to join all-party talks on September 15.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who has spearheaded efforts to reactivate peace moves since sweeping to power on May 1, made clear he would scrutinise the IRA decision to ensure that the ceaefire was genuine.

Struggling to keep suspicious pro-British Protestant leaders on a negotiating course with their Sinn Fein foes, Blair said he hoped the announcement would herald a future free of violence and despair in Northern Ireland.
"Obviously we will want to assess the ceasefire with great care. What we and others want to see is an end to violence for good and an irrevocable commitment to peaceful means," he said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, a firm supporter of Anglo-Irish demands for an IRA truce, called the impending ceasefire an historic opportunity and pledged support to build on it.

"This is a moment of great possibility," he said in a statement. "As Northern Ireland leaders begin to shape their future, I urge them to do so on the basis of the principles of fairness and compromise that underpin all democratic systems."
The IRA in a statement issued in Dublin declared it was commited to ending British sovereignty in Northern Ireland which it dubbed "the root cause" of current conflict.
"We want a permanent peace and therefore we are prepared to enhance the search for a democratic peace settlement through real and inclusive negotations," it said.
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams, in an unprecedented disclosure on Friday, said he had approached the IRA to urge an immediate end to violence.

Adams said he was satisfied that Britain and Ireland were committed to unconditional all-party talks involving Sinn Fein which would not be blocked by long-standing British and Protestant Unionist demands for an early surrender of IRA weapons.
He described the ceasefire decision as momentous and courageous and he appealed to Protestant politicians to join his party in the quest for an agreed settlement.

"Mr Blair has a responsibility to be part of the partnership for peace which must be brought about and which must be consolidated if we are to have a democratic peace settlement," Adams told a crowded news conference.

Hardline Unionist politicians poured scorn on the ceasefire announcement, portraying it as a ruse to win further concessions from London. Moderate Unionists were guarded, saying they would believe it genuine when the IRA scrapped its weapons.
Powerful Unionist leader David Trimble, riled by what he says are vague Anglo-Irish plans to secure guerrilla disarmament, meets Blair in London on Monday to press for a tougher stance.

The current multi-party talks, from which Sinn Fein was barred, would be thrown into disarray if Trimble's Ulster Unionist Party voted against the arms proposals at a vital talks session in Belfast next Wednesday.
